items.q: A program times a download. Which clock should it read at the start and at the end, and why?
options: time.time(), because it is the clock of the wall
time.monotonic() or time.perf_counter(), because they never go backwards
datetime.now(), because it has a time zone
rationales: time() can be set back by the operating system or by a time service, so the difference of two readings can be negative.
datetime.now() reads the same adjustable wall clock and, without an argument, has no time zone at all.
With a time zone argument the result is aware, so the text ends with the offset +00:00.
The Unix epoch is 1970, not 1900.

items.q: How many days are in (datetime(2026, 3, 1) - datetime(2026, 1, 1)).days?
rationales: January has 31 days and February 2026 has 28, so the difference is 59.
A timedelta has no months: the subtraction gives days (59), not 2 months.

rationales: The slashes of the format do not match the hyphens of the text, so nothing is parsed.
strptime either returns a datetime or raises; it never returns None.
%I is the hour on a 12-hour clock, so 16 becomes 04.
%p gives AM or PM in capitals in the C locale, and %I pads the hour to two digits.

items.q: datetime(2026, 1, 1) < datetime(2026, 1, 2, tzinfo=timezone.utc) is evaluated. What happens?
options: It raises TypeError, because a naive and an aware datetime cannot be compared
rationales: The comparison is refused, so no value is returned.
The comparison is refused, so no value is returned.

items.q: With ZoneInfo('America/Los_Angeles'), what is the UTC offset of 12:00 on 1 July 2026 and of 12:00 on 1 January 2026?
rationales: The zone observes daylight saving time: in July it is PDT, UTC-7.
The offsets are the other way round: the summer time of Los Angeles is UTC-7.

items.q: subprocess.run(['echo', 'hi'], shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout is what, on Linux?
rationales: With shell=True and a list, only the first item is the command and the rest are arguments of the shell itself, so echo prints an empty line.
The command runs; it just does not receive 'hi'.

items.q: What do round(2.5) and round(3.5) return?
rationales: Python rounds a half to the even neighbour, so 2.5 goes down.
3.5 goes up to 4, the even neighbour.

items.q: str(math.factorial(100000)) raises ValueError on a default Python. Why?
options: The number is larger than a float
Converting an integer of more than 4300 digits to text is refused by default
rationales: Python integers have no upper size; the float limit is not involved.
The call to factorial succeeds; it is the conversion to a string that is limited, and sys.set_int_max_str_digits() changes the limit.

items.q: In a crontab line, what does 0 9 * * 1-5 mean?
options: at 09:00 on every day of the month
rationales: The fifth field restricts the days of the week to 1 to 5, Monday to Friday.
The first field is the minute (0) and the second the hour (9); it is not an interval.
